title: Oglebay Norton Co. v. Armco, Inc.
lead: A decades-long dedicated shipping arrangement outlasts both pricing mechanisms, and evidence of continuing commitment supports a reasonable seasonal rate and supervised future negotiations.

actors.name: Oglebay Norton Company
actors.role: Great Lakes carrier committed to maintaining Armco shipping capacity.

actors.name: Armco, Inc.
actors.role: Steel company obliged to use the dedicated capacity and challenging continued enforceability.

proceedings: The trial court fixed the 1986 rate at $6.25 per gross ton and required negotiation and mediation for future disputes.
The Ohio Supreme Court affirmed continuing intent, price, and equitable supervision.
limits: The $6.25 price applied to 1986, not every season through 2010. The service contract used sales-law principles by analogy. The subpoena observation was not a separate reversal or discovery holding.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The parties repeatedly extend a dedicated shipping relationship
sections.cue: What were the original pricing mechanisms meant to serve?
paragraphs: In 1957 Oglebay agreed to maintain Great Lakes iron-ore shipping capacity for Armco, which agreed to use it. Rates first followed regular seasonal net contract rates recognized by leading ore shippers. If none existed, the parties would agree using comparable rates of leading independent operators. They selected two methods rather than leaving price entirely unexplained.

The assigned introduction describes four modifications over twenty-three years, each extending the relationship and demanding major Oglebay investment. The fourth ran through 2010, after which Oglebay began $95 million in improvements. Through 1983 the parties used Skillings Mining Review’s published rate; following an industry downturn they agreed on 1984 rates, but later could not agree. Oglebay sought declaratory relief in April 1986; Armco eventually counterclaimed unenforceability. Performance continued during suit.

No new published benchmark remained. Armco said independent rates were no longer public, and the trial court quashed nonparty rate subpoenas. Both designated mechanisms failed. Armco argued assent to those methods did not authorize a judicial substitute.

sections.title: The trial court supplies a seasonal price and a recurring negotiation process
sections.cue: What did Armco challenge on appeal?
paragraphs: After trial the court set $6.25 per gross ton for 1986. For future seasons the parties had to notify it of impasse; a mediator would be appointed and chief executives required to meet toward a rate. The court of appeals affirmed. Armco challenged intent to stay bound after mechanism failure, legal and evidentiary authority for the price, and continuing equitable supervision through 2010.

The Ohio Supreme Court treated the questions as mixed law and fact and asked whether competent, credible evidence supported critical findings. Its per curiam opinion did not simply choose its preferred price or announce that all long contracts should survive.

sections.title: The record supports commitment beyond the failed machinery
sections.cue: Why was this an existing bargain with a gap rather than future negotiations without agreement?
paragraphs: The parties’ long, close relationship included joint ventures, interlocking directors, and Armco ownership of Oglebay stock. The agreement recognized Armco’s vital and unique interest in a dedicated bulk fleet potentially carrying 7.1 million gross tons annually. Those facts supported the trial finding that capacity and continuing transport were central obligations, with pricing serving them rather than unconditionally defining their existence.

The investments described in the assignment illustrate the commercial stakes, but investment alone did not authorize imposed terms. The supported finding of ongoing contractual intent was essential. Failure of a benchmark would not always permit substitution against contrary intent.

Restatement § 33 and its comments permitted an otherwise binding bargain to gain definition from usage, dealing, implication, or a legally supplied term. A market or third-party measure that never materializes could support reasonable completion, paralleling Uniform Commercial Code § 2-305. Ohio authority used that open-price principle by analogy for services. This was a shipping-services agreement, not a directly governed goods sale.

sources.pinpoint: Continuing intent; Price gap; 52 Ohio St. 3d 235–237

sections.title: Comparative evidence supports $6 plus a self-unloading allowance
sections.cue: Why was the selected rate more than an arbitrary compromise?
paragraphs: The trial court used $6 per gross ton and twenty-five cents for self-unloading vessels, considering course of dealing, each side’s detriment, comparisons, and the depressed steel economy. An expert supported $7.44. Armco paid $5 in 1985 when the publication showed $7.41; Oglebay quoted $5.66 for 1987; LTV paid $7.41 before bankruptcy renegotiation; American Steamship quoted Armco $5.90 for 1986. The $6.25 selection lay within a supported range.

Those concrete comparisons and history justified reasonable completion; the Court did not authorize any midpoint between bargaining demands. Its footnote said protected nonparty rate information might have helped and found the reasons for quashing subpoenas unclear. That observation neither reversed the subpoena ruling nor created an independent discovery holding.

sources.pinpoint: Reasonable price; Judicial footnote; 52 Ohio St. 3d 236–237, 235 n.4

sections.title: Long-term uncertainty supports continued equitable oversight
sections.cue: What did affirmance require for later seasons?
paragraphs: Restatement § 362 required sufficiently certain obligations for specific relief, but ordinary interpretation and supplied terms had to be tried before finding fatal uncertainty. Changing markets and decades of duration made future damages too speculative. A 1962 amendment had itself allowed Armco to seek specific performance of Oglebay’s obligations, supporting reciprocal equitable treatment in this unusual relationship.

Negotiation and mediation provided a practical process to perform existing obligations rather than add or subtract major commitments. The order did not freeze the 1986 rate through 2010 or give a mediator unlimited authority to rewrite the business arrangement.

The Ohio Supreme Court affirmed on all three issues: continuing intent, supported 1986 rate, and future equitable jurisdiction. Chief Justice Moyer and Justices Sweeney, Holmes, Douglas, Wright, H. Brown, and Resnick all joined without separate writing. The case distinguishes uncertainty in an existing contract’s machinery from uncertainty over whether a binding agreement was ever made.
